title: Microsoft AI’s in-house RL framework Rocket is post-training the 3-trillion-parameter MAI Base 2
summary: If you’ve ever wondered how a large model gradually learns to “think” late in training, Microsoft AI is here to talk about the framework behind the scenes. It’s called Rocket, and it’s now being used to post-train the 3-trillion-parameter base model MAI Base 2 — not by copying answers from other models, but by letting the model climb through its own trial and error over thousands of steps and weeks at a time.
ai_summary: Microsoft AI has published a post about Rocket, its in-house reinforcement learning (RL) framework, which is being used to post-train the 3-trillion-parameter base model MAI Base 2. The approach is to “climb from the base model directly through RL” rather than distill from third-party models. Because this kind of training runs continuously for thousands of training steps, lasts weeks to months, and occupies thousands of GPUs, Rocket treats three problems as primary design constraints: stale samples, numerical inconsistency between sampler and learner, and hardware failures plus elastic scaling over long runs. To make co-design easier, Microsoft controls the learner, Rocket, and an inference engine built on a self-maintained SGLang fork. The post is aimed at engineers and researchers working on large-model training infrastructure; it focuses on system design and gives no benchmark scores, training cost, or completion timeline.
brief: Rocket previously post-trained MAI Base 1 into the reasoning model MAI Thinking 1, and has now been scaled up to train the larger MAI Base 2.
Microsoft stresses that MAI Base 2 is climbing through RL “without distillation from third-party models,” and that this work is separate from MAI Code 2.
These long runs involve thousands of training steps, weeks to months, and thousands of GPUs, so the system must survive hardware failures online and adjust its configuration as it goes.
Inference runs on a Microsoft-maintained SGLang fork; Rocket assigns nodes via Kubernetes or Slurm, and its components run as Ray actors.

sections.h: What this is: Microsoft is using its own Rocket framework to post-train the 3-trillion-parameter MAI Base 2

blocks.p: Reinforcement learning (RL) — training where a model repeatedly tries to solve tasks and adjusts its policy based on rewards — is a common late-stage step in large-model training. Microsoft AI’s post is about the infrastructure underneath that step: its in-house RL framework Rocket, and the full system built around it.

The post frames “long, stable, and numerically accurate RL” as a key step on MAI’s path to what it calls Humanist Superintelligence (Microsoft’s own term). The core idea is not to run a short RL phase at the end of post-training, but to let the model climb its capabilities through RL from the base-model stage onward.

The main subject is MAI Base 2: Microsoft’s recently announced new base model with 3 trillion parameters. The post says it is now being post-trained by Rocket on a path of “climbing from the base model through RL” without distillation from third-party models (distillation means having the model first learn from a stronger teacher model, giving it a much higher starting point).

For context: Rocket is not new. In the MAI Thinking 1 technical report, it was the framework that post-trained the previous base model MAI Base 1 into the reasoning model MAI Thinking 1. Now it has been upgraded to the larger scale MAI Base 2 requires. This work is separate from the MAI Code 2 models.

sections.h: Why skipping distillation and climbing from scratch makes infrastructure harder

blocks.p: Microsoft starts with a variable that is easy to overlook: distillation. If a model has been distilled from a stronger teacher, it enters RL already close to its ability ceiling, so RL becomes a relatively short refinement phase. In that regime, infrastructure priorities are very different: if a run fails, you can simply restart it, and small mismatches between sampler and learner don’t have time to compound into serious problems.

Rocket is designed for the harder case: starting from base capabilities and climbing entirely through RL, without the head start distillation provides. This kind of long run has to execute thousands of training steps continuously, last weeks to months, and occupy thousands of GPUs. Microsoft says being able to reach the frontier without depending on other labs’ models is central to MAI’s self-sufficiency. In this setting, the challenges above move from edge cases to primary design constraints: hardware failures are almost certain, small numerical errors accumulate over thousands of updates, and the best data mix and GPU allocation shift as the policy improves.

sections.h: The three hardest engineering problems: staleness, numerical mismatch, and failures

blocks.p: Microsoft groups the problems of scaling RL into three areas. The first is staleness: a single agent rollout (one execution in which the model tries to complete a problem) can run for hours while the learner keeps updating the policy during that time. GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization, an algorithm that computes “advantage” by comparing rewards across multiple rollouts of the same problem) scores the attempts on the same problem against one another, so if one rollout is slow or fails, it holds back the whole group and training drifts further from the current policy.

The second is numerical consistency. Fitting larger models and longer contexts into the sampler often requires lower-precision storage; if precision, kernels (the low-level compute kernels), and parallelism differ between sampler and learner, that can slow learning or even destabilize training.

The third is fault tolerance and elasticity. When thousands of GPUs run continuously for weeks to months, hardware failures will happen; at the same time, the best runtime configuration and data mix also change. If every failure or reconfiguration requires restarting the whole job, GPU time is wasted. So the system must recover components and reallocate resources while the run continues.

sections.h: Rocket’s training loop: how one problem gets worked through

blocks.p: Figure 1 in the original post shows Rocket’s asynchronous training loop. I’ve simplified it into a single path: the controller first selects a problem from a “problem pool / curriculum” and sends it to a problem worker; the problem worker then dispatches a set of rollout requests to the rollout worker pool.

Rollout workers run the agent loop: the model generates an action, the action is executed in the environment (sandbox, external tools), an observation comes back, and the loop continues to the next step. Each rollout has a per-rollout grader, and scores and references are sent back. The sampler is responsible for producing tokens — it has a router on CPU and runs SGLang on GPU for prefill and decode (the prefill and decoding steps of generation). Finally, the learner updates the policy on a GPU pool.

sections.h: Why build the learner, Rocket, and SGLang together

blocks.p: Microsoft stresses that RL needs three tightly connected systems: the learner and training framework (Rocket), and an inference engine built on a Microsoft-maintained SGLang fork. Owning all three lets the teams design the interfaces between them rather than optimizing each component in isolation.

That doesn’t mean every layer is written from scratch. Rocket uses Kubernetes or Slurm to allocate nodes to a job, and its components run as Ray actors. On the inference side, it starts from open-source SGLang but makes substantial changes to fit MAI’s models and long-running agentic RL workloads — where the model acts autonomously over many steps. Microsoft says a future blog post will detail those SGLang changes.

So why not use an existing open-source framework? The post names verl and slime, saying they provide a solid foundation for distributed execution, customizable agent workflows, and asynchronous sampling. But Microsoft’s “long climb from a base model” pushes these frameworks into a regime they aren’t usually tested in, so Microsoft built Rocket and designed its infrastructure around its own RL workloads and models.

list: No specific compute cost, GPU model, or GPU count for Rocket or MAI Base 2 post-training.
No benchmark scores or comparison targets for MAI Base 2 after Rocket post-training.
No exact figures for “thousands of training steps,” “thousands of GPUs,” or “weeks to months.”
No timeline for when this post-training will finish or when the post-trained model will be available.
No detail on how MAI Code 2 relates to this RL work, beyond saying the two are independent.
No specific GRPO hyperparameters, such as learning rate or batch size.

blocks.p: The post’s value is in explaining the design thinking behind a large-scale RL training system: why long-run RL is harder than a short refinement phase, how the three major challenges shape system design, and the tradeoffs between building your own framework and using open-source ones. For engineers and researchers building RL post-training pipelines, or trying to understand large-model training infrastructure, the most useful ideas are “build the three systems together” and “design fault tolerance around long climbs.”

The tradeoff is that it stays at the system-overview level: no code, no reproducible configuration, and no performance data. If you’re hoping to read how capable MAI Base 2 is, you’ll be disappointed — that will have to wait for a post-trained release or a technical report.

Concrete advice: if you’re building an RL training system, focus on the three major challenges and the CPU/GPU division of labor. If you care about model capability, this post can’t give you a verdict; wait for the post-trained MAI Base 2. If you’re just a regular user, this is mostly behind-the-scenes engineering and won’t change your everyday product experience.
